fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think benchmarks play a really interesting role, and it's actually evolved a lot over the last few years. For a long time in machine learning, benchmarks were sort of the scoreboard, right? You'd have ImageNet or GLUE or whatever, and the community would hill-climb on it, and that was how we measured progress. And that was useful, but it also led to a lot of overfitting to the benchmark itself rather than to the actual capability we cared about.

What I think has changed with things like SWE-bench and tau-bench and WebShop is that the benchmark itself becomes a kind of specification for what we want the system to do. So with SWE-bench, the question wasn't "can the model complete a code snippet," it was "can the model take a real GitHub issue from a real repository, navigate the codebase, figure out where the problem is, make a change, and have the tests pass." That's a lot closer to what an actual software engineer does. And when we released it, the best models were solving under two percent of the tasks. Now they're solving a large majority of them. And I don't think that progress would have happened as fast if the target hadn't been made concrete.

WebShop was kind of the earlier version of that same idea for me. We wanted to see whether a language agent could actually operate in a web-like environment, search for products, read descriptions, click through options, and buy the right thing. At the time, the dominant setups for agents were text games or very synthetic environments, and we wanted something that was grounded in real data and real user instructions. A lot of what we learned there about how agents get stuck, how they fail to recover, how they don't explore enough, carried over into later work.

And tau-bench came out of looking at what happens when you put these agents in front of actual users, in customer service settings for example. There you have a policy the agent has to follow, you have a human on the other side who's often ambiguous or changes their mind, and you have tools and databases the agent needs to interact with. One of the things we found there, which I think is really important, is that reliability is a huge gap. Even when a model succeeds once on a task, if you run it eight times, the probability it succeeds all eight times drops off dramatically. And that's the metric that actually matters if you're going to deploy something.

So the way I think about it now is, a good benchmark should do three things. It should be close enough to the real task that progress on it means something. It should be hard enough that the current systems don't saturate it immediately. And it should surface failure modes that you wouldn't have noticed otherwise, so it's not just a number, it's a diagnostic. If you get those right, the benchmark almost acts like a forcing function. People build towards it, the capabilities improve, and then you have to go build the next one. That's kind of the cycle we're in, and honestly I think it's been one of the healthier dynamics in the field.

r001.rationale: The response says these benchmarks specify real tasks, describing SWE-bench as handling real GitHub issues and WebShop as finding and buying products, and contrasts WebShop with text games and synthetic environments.

opus-5.5.text:
I think benchmarks play an outsized role in AI, maybe more than in most fields, because they define what people work on. A good benchmark is a statement about what matters. So when we built these, the question was always: what capability do we actually want these systems to have, and how do we measure it in a way that's faithful to the real world while still being automatically evaluable at scale?

Take WebShop. This was around 2021–2022, before agents were a big buzzword. We wanted to know whether a language model could take a fuzzy human instruction, like "I want a pair of waterproof hiking boots under a hundred dollars," and go into a realistic website environment, search, click around, compare options, and buy the right thing. We built it with over a million real products so it had real messiness, but it was still a controlled environment where we could reward the agent automatically. At the time, models were pretty bad at it, and that gap was the point. It gave people something concrete to push on.

SWE-bench came from a similar philosophy. Coding benchmarks then were mostly self-contained puzzles, write a function that does X, and models were starting to saturate them. Real software engineering looks nothing like that. You get a GitHub issue, you have to navigate a big codebase you didn't write, figure out where the problem is, and make a change that doesn't break anything else. So we took real issues and the pull requests that resolved them from popular Python repositories, and used the repositories' own tests as the check. When we released it, the best models solved only a couple percent of the tasks, and a lot of people thought it was too hard to be useful. Then it became one of the main yardsticks for coding agents, and progress went from low single digits to well over half in a fairly short time. That's what a good benchmark does: it's hard but not impossible, and it's tied to something people genuinely care about.

Tau-bench, which we did with folks at Sierra, targets something the others don't fully capture: an agent interacting with a human user while following a domain policy and using tools, say a customer service agent for an airline or a retailer. There are two things I think are important there. One is that the user is part of the loop. We simulate the user with a language model, so the conversation is dynamic, and the agent has to gather information and handle ambiguity. The other is reliability. We introduced a metric called pass^k, which asks whether the agent succeeds consistently across multiple trials of the same task, not just once. In real deployments, being right 60% of the time isn't good enough if a business is putting this in front of millions of customers. What we saw was that reliability drops off quite sharply as you increase k, even for strong models. That's a sobering signal, and I think it's pushed the field to think about consistency, not just peak performance.

The broader lesson is that benchmarks have a lifecycle. They're most valuable when they're unsaturated and well aligned with real use cases. Once models start doing really well, you have to ask whether you're measuring the capability or just overfitting to the benchmark, through contamination, or people tuning their systems specifically for it. So I see benchmark-building as an ongoing process: you build something that captures a real gap, the community makes progress, and then you go find the next gap. Right now I think the frontier is longer-horizon tasks, more open-ended environments, and evaluation that captures things like cost, safety, and reliability, not just whether the task got done.

r001.rationale: The response presents WebShop as realistic shopping and SWE-bench as real software engineering, contrasting the latter with self-contained coding puzzles. It frames these benchmarks as measuring capabilities tied to real-world use.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me. Benchmarks have always been a huge driver of progress in AI, going back to ImageNet in computer vision or GLUE and SQuAD in NLP. But I think the benchmarks you mentioned represent a shift in what we're measuring, and that shift matters a lot.

The older generation of benchmarks mostly tested static, single-shot capabilities — can the model classify this sentence, can it answer this question. What we tried to do with WebShop, and later with SWE-Bench, was move toward evaluating agents: systems that have to operate in an environment, take sequences of actions, observe feedback, and work toward a goal over many steps. In WebShop, the model has to actually navigate a simulated e-commerce site, search, click, read product pages, and buy the right item. In SWE-Bench, it has to resolve real GitHub issues from real repositories — understand a large codebase, localize the problem, write a patch, and pass the tests. And something like TAU-Bench pushes on another dimension, which is interacting with a human user while following policies and using tools, which is much closer to what deployed agents actually face.

I'd say these benchmarks serve a few roles. First, they ground our claims about capability. It's easy to be impressed by demos, but demos are cherry-picked. When SWE-Bench came out, the best models were solving under two percent of issues, and that was a sobering, useful signal about the gap between "writes plausible code" and "does real software engineering." Second, they give the field a shared hill to climb. A lot of the progress in agent scaffolding, tool use, and long-horizon reasoning over the past couple of years has been driven directly by people competing on these tasks. And third, they expose failure modes you'd never see in static evaluation — error recovery, compounding mistakes over long trajectories, grounding language in actual actions.

That said, I'd add two cautions. One is that benchmarks have a lifespan — once they become targets, you get contamination and overfitting, and the numbers start to mean less than they did. We've had to think hard about things like held-out, verified subsets for exactly this reason. The other is that no benchmark fully captures the messiness of the real world. Real users are ambiguous, real environments change, and the cost of errors isn't uniform. So I see these benchmarks as necessary instruments — they tell us where we are and focus the community's effort — but the real goal is building systems that are robust beyond the benchmark, and we have to keep designing new evaluations that stay ahead of the models.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from static, single-shot benchmarks toward agent tasks, including real GitHub issues and scenarios closer to deployed agents. It does not characterize that shift as moving beyond game-playing, so the full stated contrast is missing.

opus-5.text:
I think benchmarks are the single most underrated driver of progress in this field, and also one of the most misunderstood.

The honest history is that whatever we measure is what gets optimized. When we built WebShop back in 2022, the motivation was pretty simple: language models were getting good at text, but there was no way to ask whether they could actually *do* anything. We wanted an environment with a real action space, real consequences, a reward you couldn't talk your way into. And it turned out that framing — put the model in a loop with an environment — was more important than the particular task. WebShop looks quaint now, but the shape of it is everywhere.

SWE-Bench was the same instinct applied to something people actually care about. The insight there was that we didn't have to invent tasks; GitHub had millions of them, with tests attached, which gives you verification for free. That's the thing I'd tell anyone building a benchmark today: find the domain where the grading is already done for you by reality.

But I'd push back on the idea that benchmarks are just scoreboards. The interesting failure is that a number on a leaderboard tells you almost nothing about whether you can deploy the thing. That's really why we did τ-bench — once you put a user in the loop, and a policy the agent is supposed to follow, you discover that models are wildly inconsistent. Run the same task eight times and you get different outcomes. So we reported pass^k instead of pass@k, because for a customer service agent, being right eighty percent of the time isn't eighty percent of the value — it might be zero. Reliability is a different axis than capability, and we'd been collapsing them.

The other thing I'd say is that benchmarks have a shelf life, and that's fine. They saturate, they get contaminated, people overfit. The useful question isn't "how do we build the permanent benchmark," it's "what's the next thing we can't measure yet." Right now I think that's long-horizon work — tasks that take a human days, where there's no clean unit test at the end. We don't really know how to evaluate that, and until we do, I'd be skeptical of anyone claiming their agent can do it.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Benchmarks matter a lot, probably more than people give them credit for. They define the target the whole field is aiming at. If you look at how progress happens in AI, it's usually that someone builds a good measuring stick, and then a lot of people pile onto it and push.

The three you mentioned came from a particular motivation. Language models were getting very good at static tasks like question answering and classification, but we wanted to know whether they could *act*: take a goal, interact with an environment over many steps, use tools, and recover from mistakes. WebShop was an early attempt at that. It's a simulated e-commerce site where the agent has to read a natural-language instruction like "find me a blue jacket under fifty dollars," then search, click, compare options, and buy. It was a cheap, scalable way to study grounded language agents before we had models that could really do this.

SWE-Bench took the same idea and made it much more real. Instead of a toy environment, you take actual GitHub issues from actual open-source repos and ask whether the model can produce a patch that makes the tests pass. When we released it, models solved a couple of percent of the tasks. Now we're at numbers that would have seemed unreasonable then. I think part of why it took off is that the task is something people really care about, so progress on it feels meaningful rather than just a number going up.

Tau-bench looks at something different, which is the interaction between an agent, a user, and a set of tools and policies. Think of a customer service setting where the agent has to follow rules, like what it can refund or when it needs to verify something, while talking to a simulated user who might be vague or change their mind. What I like about it is that it pushes on reliability. It's not enough to get it right once. If you run the same task many times, does the agent get it right consistently? For deployment, that gap between "can sometimes do it" and "does it dependably" is huge.

I'd add a few caveats, though. Benchmarks saturate, and once a number gets high, it stops telling you much. There's also contamination and over-optimization, where people start tuning specifically for the benchmark rather than for the underlying capability. And no benchmark fully captures the messiness of the real world. So I see them as a living thing. You have to keep building harder, more realistic ones as models improve, and treat them as one signal rather than the whole story.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving beyond static question answering and classification toward interactive tasks, including real GitHub issues and customer service. It does not characterize this shift as moving beyond game-playing, so the full criterion is not communicated.

haiku-5.5.text:
Benchmarks matter a lot, but I think of them as a way to point the field in a direction, not as a finish line. A good benchmark gives people a shared, concrete target, and that's how a lot of progress actually happens. WebShop was useful for that reason. It forced agents to deal with messy, partially observable web pages, search, and a long sequence of decisions, which is very different from answering a single prompt.

SWE-bench moved things further toward real work. Resolving actual GitHub issues in real codebases is a much more meaningful test than a multiple-choice score, and it exposed how much of the difficulty lies in navigating a repository, reasoning across files, and checking your own changes. τ-bench pushes in another direction. It's about multi-turn conversations with a simulated user, following policies, and using tools correctly. I think its reliability-oriented measures are especially important, because an agent that succeeds once in a while isn't something you can deploy.

The risks are real, though. Once a benchmark becomes the thing everyone optimizes, scores can rise without the underlying capability rising in the same way. You see this through contamination, overfitting to a particular harness, and small quirks in how success is scored. Benchmarks also saturate quickly, so the field keeps needing harder and more realistic ones.

So my view is that benchmarks are essential, but they're most useful when we're honest about what they measure, when we report cost and variance alongside accuracy, and when we check them against how systems behave in the real settings people care about.

astra-6.text:
I think benchmarks like these are really valuable because they make progress concrete. We can say we want an AI system that helps people accomplish things, but then we have to ask: What does accomplishing a task actually mean? How do we measure success? A benchmark gives us a shared target and a way to compare different approaches.

What interests me particularly is evaluating the whole process of solving a task. Can the system decide what to do next, take an action, interpret the feedback, and recover when something goes wrong? Those capabilities can be difficult to capture with a single question and answer. And looking at where a system fails can be more useful than just looking at its overall score, because that tells us what we need to work on.

But I would also be careful about equating progress on a benchmark with solving the broader problem. Any benchmark captures a particular slice of what we care about. You want to know whether improvements carry over to unfamiliar tasks and situations, and whether the system remains reliable when the conditions change. So I see these benchmarks as essential research tools, but the goal should always be the capability behind the benchmark, rather than the score itself.

r001.rationale: The response presents benchmarks as measuring practical task-solving and helping people accomplish things, but it does not communicate that they push evaluation beyond game-playing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very useful because they give us concrete ways to measure whether these systems can actually accomplish tasks. With an agent, you care about the whole process: can it make a plan, interact with an environment, use the feedback it gets, and recover when something goes wrong? Benchmarks give researchers a common setting in which to study those capabilities and compare approaches.

They’re also useful for discovering what’s missing. You can look at a failed task and ask whether the problem was reasoning, exploration, or keeping track of information over multiple steps. That can lead to much more specific research questions.

But I think we have to keep asking what a benchmark score tells us about performance outside that particular setting. As systems improve, we need new tasks, variations, and more realistic conditions. So I see benchmarks as essential tools for guiding progress, with the understanding that any individual benchmark captures only part of what we want an intelligent system to do.

luna-6.text:
I see them as useful milestones because they push us beyond asking whether a model can produce a good answer and toward whether it can actually complete a task. SWE-Bench asks whether a system can make a change in a codebase; TAO-Bench and WebShop look at how it handles multi-step interactions with tools and online environments. Those settings expose failures that simpler question-and-answer tests can miss: keeping track of a goal, choosing the right action, and recovering when something goes wrong.

But a benchmark is still only a slice of reality. We have to watch for systems learning the test rather than the underlying skill, and for a score hiding important differences in reliability or how much human help was needed. The best use of these benchmarks is to make progress visible and point to what still breaks, alongside broader evaluation with varied tasks and real users.
